To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
AI/ML academic literature, Canadian newspaper articles, and Twitter tweets do not engage with disabled people in ways that are meaningful to them and that are in line with their rights.
AI/ML literature, Canadian newspaper articles, and Twitter tweets, mostly engage with disabled people as potential therapeutic and/or non-therapeutic users of AI/ ML influenced products.
AI/ML literature and Canadian newspaper and Twitter coverage of AI/ML engages with disabled people as therapeutic or non-therapeutic users of AI/ ML influenced products.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how disabled people are engaged with in relation to AI/ML within academic literature, Canadian English language newspapers, and Twitter.

the extent to which the academic literature, Canadian newspaper articles, and Twitter tweets covering AI and ML engage with the concept of "disabled people" as well as the extent to which disabled people are engaged with in relation to their roles as users of, and knowledge producers and influencers of AI/ ML discourses.
the extent to which disabled people are engaged with within AI/ML discources.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the coverage of disabled people and AI/ML is very limited and that the focus of this coverage is on the therapeutic and non therapeutic use of AI/ ML influenced products and technologies.
AI/ML discursive spaces are not inclusive of disabled people, and that disabled people are not meaningfully engaged with in AI/ML discoursive spaces

disabled people are not covered in AI/ML literature and in the Canadian newspapers and Twitter as knowledge contributors and influencers of AI/ ML discourses including AI/M governance and ethics discources, that they are mostly depicted as therapeutic and non therapeutic AI/ML users and that they are not covered as stakeholders in AI/ML discoursed.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
disabled people are not covered in the AI/ML discursive landscape in a manner commensurate with their stake in AI/ML.
the current AI/ML coverage is not inclusive of disabled people and that disabled people are under-represented in AI/ML discources.
the coverage of AI/ML within academic literature, Canadian English language newspapers and tweets is mostly techno optimistic.
The main takeaway from our work is that
disabled people are mostly engaged with as therapeutic or non therapeutic AI/ML influenced product users.
disabled people are mostly engaged with in AI/ML discoursing as therapeutic and non therapeutic AI/ML users.
AI/ML is not being covered as a social good for disabled people.
